sentences.text: Oh, I just see your note here.
Yeah, sorry, a couple minutes late here.
Just running from.
From another call.
We're in full, full planning mode for NFL draft, so just a lot of fires already.
Yeah, thanks for taking time.
Yeah, no worries at all.
Yeah, just some people are a little bit late and then they're not going to turn up, so you always got to ping, ping them just in case.
You guys in New York, but Jersey.
City, right across the Hudson.
Not far.
Yep, same area.
Yeah.
What about yourself?
We're London based, but we've got a team in New York and Los Angeles as well, so.
Okay.
Well, you're a lot closer your weekend than we are, but we're all on the same day though.
Friday.
Exactly.
Exactly.
We're 55 minutes away from going to the pub.
Let's not be the, the group that holds you back from that.
Yeah, exactly.
Don't drag it out for me.
Good to see you guys.
Good to meet you.
I got you a Note, Leighton.
Through LinkedIn, wasn't it?
And then we set up a call together, so.
Yeah.
Yeah, I just, I came across your name and some others in an article in Digiday and as an early stage agency we just launched January of last year.
We've always got an eye for those types of transactions as we're, you know, thinking and, and idea around how to scale the agency.
Connecting with like minded folks, folks who are active in the marketplace as evident by that Digiday article.
That includes yourself.

Just to connect and kind of learn more about, you know, what each other do and what we, what we do here at Gray Wolf as well and, and just see, you know, keep in touch for the future should something, you know, an opportunity arise, whether it's strategic investment or some sort of transaction that helps us scale further down the line.
Just.
That was the impetus for reaching out.
Yeah.
Okay, cool.
Yeah, we could.
To get a good idea on what it is that you guys do.
I mean even if you're early stage, you kind of, you never know really.
There's a, there's a transaction waiting for everybody.
I'm just a bit about us then.
We're capital A group.
We're an M and A advisory.
We specialize in marketing and media agencies.
So we help agencies find ideal buyers or acquisition targets.
So we work both buy and the sell side.
On the buy side, we tend to work mostly with agencies, but sometimes directly with private equity firms or investors or agencies that they've already invested in.
We're helping them to grow.
We also own and operate agencies co which is a marketplace for agency owners to buy and sell agencies as well.
So that's our sell side thing.
The last 12 months, we've helped agencies close over 50 million in transactions, obviously working in sports as well as lots of other verticals.
So we work buy and sell right across our network.
So subscribers to agencies co, we've got 20,000 subscribers there and 130,000 marketing agencies in our CRM.
So we've got a lot going on around us all the time.

So, yeah, it'd be great to understand more about your agency and what your goals are and see if there's a fit with any of our buyers at the moment or whether it's, you know, something that's, you know, exploratory for potential exit strategy in the future.
That's all good as well.
Yeah, certainly a future.
Future opportunity.
Yeah.
So Sean and I, we launched Greywolf January of last year.
And before that we worked together at Endeavor, which is large sports entertainment conglomerate, owns a UFC, WWE, etc.
And so we ideated in early 2023 around how the PR industry specifically was evolving as a result of the ever shifting media landscape.
And we were fortunate enough to have a bit of proof of concept out of the gate.

We launched with Toyota as a client working specifically on their NFL business, and then kind of started building the agency around that scope of work, which was very heavily in the partnership space with the NFL.
Yeah, and when we say partnership, we're usually referring to sponsorship, and in often cases it's sports sponsorship.
But any ways that a brand could get an external cultural amplifier is what we're focused on.
So you guys go out and you find the sponsor on behalf of your clients.
Well, that's what makes us unique.
There's many firms that do that.
We do is once the partnership is intact, we then apply our PR knowledge.
We're lifelong PR practitioners, but our time at Endeavor made us adjacent to partnership marketing.

That was a big part of why brands like Visa, Anheuser Busch, the National Football League, that's why they came to endeavors that they had some, you know, partnership that they wanted to, you know, whether it was the Olympics or what have you.
So we took that all, you know, we were on the same floor with all of the people that do that.
We were working in the same business as all of them, really servicing clients together.
So we have outsized knowledge on sponsorship marketing, but we are adjacent to that.

What we do is we design programs and strategies so that those sponsorships can be extended out through social media and through earned media so you're just taking the contractual assets, the rights that the brand purchased, and then we'll come up with ideas that extend that sponsorship into cultural resonance, which is, you know, for PR people, we would call that, you know, getting in people's social feeds and, and in the news outlets that they, they consume.
Okay.
And, and, and we're the only firm that has that positioning.

There are other firms that may do some of the things we're talking about, but their services are expansive and they might be doing crisis communications or, you know, all the areas of, of capability that PR firm might tout.
We are very comfortable in the idea that we are a niche specialist firm.
Okay, so you're working with the brand that has bought the rights, so they're leveraging those rights.
So for instance, a brand sponsors the NFL and your remit is really to then use that partnership that they've created to go out and create brand opportunities in media.
And how, what, what kind of are you focused on?
So is that social media opportunities or is that, you know, real life stuff where you're, you're doing, you know, like events or, you know, immersive interactions with the audience?
Or is it, you know, where do you focus?
How do you get the bang for your buck?
Sure, I think the easiest way to look at that is bucketing as traditional pr.
So that can mean a whole bunch of things, but it's traditional media relations.
Right.
Working hand in hand with journalists, TV broadcasters, podcasters to have them cover the partnership, its various events, et cetera.
So it's traditional media relations, it's influencer marketing.
Right.
If we're in a media market or in a situation where traditional media relations isn't going to cut, it isn't going to get the value we want.
We could also bolt on influencers to help extend visibility digitally on the partnership, the brand, its events, et cetera, and social media.
In terms of content strategy, we can help them think through creating big moments on the largest social media platforms.
Yeah.
So let's take you through an example of what we just came back from recently at the Super Bowl.
Gray Wolf was down in the super bowl for eight days.

And we designed a strategy that we executed earlier this month at the super bowl where Toyota had a branded set and we had three media partners that were broadcasting around a Toyota themed set that actually included their Toyota vehicles as part of the stage.
That was Yahoo Sports, that was the New York Times, and their athletic brand, and then Complex, which is a big urban market, urban culture site here.
And then we took the team Toyota athletes, probably the most famous of those being Eli Manning.
And we were able to bring them around to all the different media outlets at the Super Bowl.
And then we also worked in tandem with Toyota's other agencies to create this community event in New Orleans where for the first time ever, there was a glow in the dark flag football game.
And Toyota's association with flag football around the world was celebrated through that.

And then we're also working with content creators that are using social content and going around to the different Toyota fan activation areas, engaging with fans and then capturing that content on their own.
And we had some of the top content and news personalities around the world of football, American football, capturing all that to give you that qualification.
And so that's just an example of, like, what we would do for one week.

And then after the super bowl, we're trying to find opportunity that we would call unseen for many others that we're bringing an insight on our knowledge of the, the sports landscape and the media landscape.
And we're, and we're creating something that another firm might not even bring forward or catch.
And we did something like that around the holiday season where one of their Toyota players, Brock Purdy, the quarterback of the 49ers, he was, he was caught on Mike at a game.
He was just as his, his teammates were just sort of joking around and there was a timeout.
So they were just on the, on the field and they said, hey, Brock, like, like, when are you gonna give us one of those Toyotas?
You know, referring to his national marketing deal with Toyota.
And he says, oh, yeah, Toyota's.
Yeah, I'll get you.
You know, so it's just a throwaway joke.
It didn't really land that much, that much here.
But we pulled it down through our news monitoring and we shared this with Toyota.
It was like, what if we could make this real?
What if at the holidays he could give back to the guys that block for him?
And each.
The lineman gets a Toyota vehicle that, that got picked up in virtually every major news outlet here.
And it was this.

You know, we don't like to use the word viral lightly, but for people that had worked at Toyota for decades, this was one of the first instances that they could think of where the brand was being talked about organically.
And it wasn't their ad buys, it wasn't their Olympic sponsorship and Olympic rights.
It was something that, you know, the fans were sharing and passing along on their own.
And there was, you know, there was all this discussion that, did Brock pay for it?
Did Toyota Pay for it.
So fans were going back and forth, and that was all rooted in an insight that we brought to them, that this is what quarterbacks do.
They give their linemen gifts around the holidays.
It's a tradition.
So that was an example of how we're finding opportunity.
But then we're, we're scheduling.
You know, we, we know the year, you know, we know we're going to be at the super bowl, the NFL draft.
So we're also theming around these big moments that the brand can plan for.
So you're working with the assets, the brand assets that they're putting together with other partners, but you're, you're making sure they get coverage, basically.
So you're flexing either traditional media or influencers just around those brand assets to make sure that they get engagement on them.
Yep.
The brand's already purchased them.
They've already secured the rights to be an NFL partner, and they're already using people like Eli Manning to be in the commercials.
So we're just, we're just creating ideas that spin off and utilize that.
Okay, brilliant.
Wow.
Sounds really good.
And you're just working in sports.
So what's the sort of.
What's the roster look like at the moment?
Is it NFL?
Anything else that you've got?
NFL's big.
But, you know, the Toyota NFL business.
Is a big one for us, and it was, it was our anchor client out of the gate.
But we've got clients in the apparel space who are attached to ufc, which is going to be a huge future sports property here.
We've got some agencies as well on roster who do the partnership deals, but don't do the PR piece.
So we kind of in that little gap there for them, a bit of white space in that and that market as well.
And then Verizon, we've been getting a lot of projects from their regional marketing groups.
So the client is the brand.
The brand's already paid for, and you guys are the experts to make sure they get the leverage.
Yeah, and there's partnership marketing firms that secure the deals, they negotiate them, they manage the assets.
In terms of their contractual usage, we work alongside those firms.
So in this country, we know a lot of them, we know a lot of the heads of those agencies, and they don't see us as.
They're not territorial.
They see we're actually amplifying their work.
We're bringing a storytelling element and, and they're actually happy to work with us.
So how do you pitch yourselves in, guys?
You know, at what stage do you approach Toyota.
So once they've, They've.
I'm assuming they probably had a long relationship, but say that they land that relationship in with the NFL, then they're going out to agencies that are building all these opportunities for them.
They've probably got an agency of record that's, you know, doing the overall strategy.
Who comes to you, where do.
When do you get involved in that for the brand?
What's interesting about us is that we get hired by the marketing group, not the, not the communications group.
So usually there is some sort of frustration or identification of a need that comes from the marketing group that oversees the sponsorship.
And they go out and they, and they ask around and they say, who?
You know, we need someone specialized.
There's a.
There's a really great firm that serves the company for our communications work, but that could be investor relations, that could be new products, that could be executive elevation.
All the different things that a big agency would do for a big company.
But they say, we want someone specialized.
And what makes Greywolf unique is that we were admittedly specialized.
We embrace our niche, and that makes us more acceptable to other PR firms that may not turf war on us because they already have a large part of the business.
And they say, well, we don't know anything about it.
You know, Major League Baseball or NFL or, or mls.
So, yeah, look at this little firm.
They're.
They're a niche specialty firm.
So we don't.
We.
We will actually go out and we have it.
We've put it on our LinkedIn post.
We say, we are not an agency of record and we embrace it because we know that these big brands don't want to sever relationships with large agencies that serve the rest of their business.
But, you know, if everyone looks at our website and say, oh, that's all they are, they're sports specialists.
Then there's.
There's no resistance to bringing us on from the other agencies that have these deep relationships with the brand.
Right.
And so a brand like Toyota, they could have relationships across loads of niches.
You guys are just in the sports bit.
There could be something else for somebody else.
Okay, all right, let's get a sense of where you guys are at then.
Obviously it's new, but in terms of, like, size, is it just you two guys?
What kind of revenue are you at the moment?
Yeah, so right now it's the two of us full time.
We're supplemented by anywhere between five and six contractors, depending on workload across the.
Anywhere between six and seven active clients at once.
And then in terms of revenue, we will be at or hope to surpass a mil this year.
Year two in, we might be a little bit below that depending on what happens with one of our consumer tech clients at the moment.
But, yeah, we hope to be at or near or surpass the mill this year.
Yeah.
So we're bootstrapped and profitable.
Yeah.
Cool.
And the profit covers more than just you, you two seller, I guess.
Yeah, yeah.
I mean, it will be anywhere between, I think last year we finished was a 54% or 60% profit.
So we've been pretty intentional about stocking away cash as piece of every retainer that we get.
So profit is coming for us.
That's all going into your wedding this summer, Leighton?
Yes.
Yeah, exactly that.
Okay, brilliant.
All right, well, great margins at the moment, but obviously it's just you two, you guys.
So what are you looking to achieve?
What's.
What's your current goals?
You know, where are you trying to take this?
Yeah, scale.
We want a higher volume, like a longer client roster at this point.
At this point, we're trying to recreate as many Toyotas, obviously, as we, as we can across the major sports leagues in the US So client scale also headcount scale.

We want to spend more time working on the business versus in it, which means we looking for some, some probably mid to senior level talent to bring on board at this, at some point this year, start getting involved with the Toyota business and then, you know, the next blue chip in addition to Verizon as well.
And what's, what's the plan for the business?
You know?
Yeah, yeah.

The growth plan for us is that last year was, was, was launch, define our position in the industry and then create client satisfaction that we could merchandise in the form of case studies and testimonials.
So we've done that.
And now what we want to do for 2025, Greywolf is going to do more industry marketing to get our unique position out there.
There may be a lot of sponsorship marketers that just don't know that there's a specialized service out there that could take their sponsorships to the next level.
And they don't have to fire any of their existing firms to do it.
And to do that, we're going to appear at.
We've already marked what we believe are the four most influential conferences.

And what probably gets us the most excited is that we're talking to outlets and, well, Sponsor United is probably the one that we're talking to the most right now about creating a thought leadership Program where we actually define and rank the brands that are doing what we call sponsorship amplification, partnership amplification.
Who's doing that?
The best.
And we score that through data through our.
Our partner.
Again, it could be Sponsor United or another data provider, a third party, credible data source.
And then that will be our way to get brands to see how they line up in this thing that we're calling partnership amplification.
And it gets us more brand access because they want to access the report, hear more about the findings.
So that is what Greywolf has in mind for 2025 for growth.
Okay.
And then sort of ultimately, what.
What are you trying to achieve for yourselves, you know, in terms of an exit?
Are you building towards something else?
Are you building, you know, into the future forever?
Are you rolling up more companies or, you know, what's the plan?
Sell it back to endeavor.
We're young.
We're young.
So we want people to believe in the unique position, and we want people to believe that the leaders that have done it can.
Can continue to do it.
So that, that's.
But that, you know, the other thing is we're.
We're not.
We're not reaching out with an immediate need.
And that's been pretty consistent with how Leighton and I have operated.
And we will talk to a production company in, like, we worked with a production company to film some content that we did with Verizon on Monday.
We had talked to them in.
In April, and we said, guys, we don't know what we've got coming, but just wanted to refamiliar ourselves.
You know, old contact.
This is what we're doing with Greywolf.
So we're constantly, you know, it doesn't matter with staff vendors.
Like, we are always forecasting in the future.
It's just how we.
It's just how we operate.
So, you know, we just truly, like, we just thought you were a guy of interest that we wanted to connect with and just wanted to put you, you know, gray wolf to be on your consciousness.
And then this way, if there's a conversation that has to happen quicker, you know, we.
At least we know each other.
Yeah.
Yeah.
So probably what will happen over time is people will start knocking on your door and making offers.
And obviously that's a.
It's a good position to.
To be in.

But if you guys are certain that there's the right time to sell, then the best thing really to do is get the preparation done and get a team like us involved and go to market so you can speak to four or five serious buyers at the same time.
And, and then you're in the driving seat and you get to pick.
But I guess you're going to have a lot of door knockers speaking to you over the next couple of years.
Certainly I'm thinking of a couple of clients that would like to speak to you already.
But I think one of the other things to think about is what the value is that you want to exit at the moment.
If you get that 1 million in revenue this year and you've still got something close to a 50% margin, then most agencies go for, you know, a 5, 5 to 7x.
If you're in a specialty market like yours and there's a lot of growth, then it can be higher than that, you know, seven, eight, nine.
So you could already be looking at a couple of million each, you know, to, to sell this time around.
3 years working for somebody else, both of you with a million in the bank each and then you can go and start the next thing up as well.
So it might be that you're already fairly close to doing an exit.
So yeah, anyway, but those things to be decided I guess over the next few years.
Gotcha.

And just like in terms of our positioning the specialty, do you have, I mean you deal with folks like I'm sure on the regular, any knee jerk reaction to how we might be positioned based on your many conversations?
Yeah, so you're going to be attractive for a couple of different types of buyers.
So it's either going to be vertical or it's going to be service based.

So you know there's going to be companies that are already doing this kind of earned media stuff and they, they are going to want to grow either into sport in general or just, you know, the specialty that you guys are in, which is great, isn't it?
You know, there must be a ton of brands that have paid for sponsorships that need your help.
So I should imagine even if they're not interested in just the sports element of this, that they would looking to do this across a ton of different verticals.
So I think it's going to be it's either that or you're going to have companies that specialize in sports.
So obviously that's why we're having this conversation.
We've got a client where we've done two acquisitions already in the sport vertical and they're actually looking, their expertise was really in, what do they call it, Spatial computing.
So that's like VR, AR, mixed reality, immersive stuff.

So when you know, you've got fans at an event, they're looking at ways of, you know, immersing those fans in sort of tech stuff as well as whatever the real life experience is that they're getting as well.
So, so, but those are again just particularly around sports events.
So they would, you know, a company like that would want to add this sort of thing on.
They're already working with the brands and bringing some expertise in like yourself, where you're able to amplify that as well.
I mean it just goes hand in hand.
It's a no brainer that they wouldn't want to have your expertise as well.
So I think you've got a few buyers there and then depending on your size, you know, once you get to a certain size, 1 million EBITDA plus you start to get private equity as well.
Looking to make, you know, a PE play.
They would typically want, you know, like a, a company that they are going to build everything on first.

So they would buy a company like yours, but bigger and then they would look at a bunch of other businesses that were doing the same sort of thing and bolt it all together and they would then build that for three to five years and then sell the whole thing at, you know, a 10x multiple.
They're buying at 5 and selling at a 10x.
Even if they didn't do anything else apart from a small amount of organic growth, just by rolling up companies together they can sell them for way more just because they're starting to get size.
So yeah, I mean those are sort of two to three types of buyers.
The first two you're probably going to get door knocked for already and the private equity thing will come later when, I mean you're not far off.
If you can do 2 million next year and keep a 50% margin, then potentially a private equity business might be interested in speaking to you as well.
So what do you recommend in terms of communication?
How frequently should we keep in touch with you just to keep you posted on growth plans?
Yeah, I mean every sort of half year is probably a good place to start.

You know, if you guys are really building, I mean you've already done really well and if you get past that million then obviously you're a high growth business and somebody will want to buy you while you're growing.
That's kind of the play.
And also in terms of advice, don't wait until you've plateaued to go to market.
You want to sell it when you're just smashing your numbers.
So if you can continue on that growth curve over the next 12 months.
Then don't necessarily write off selling early because you'll be worth a shit ton while you're going up.
But as soon as you plateau, then those multiples start to level out as well.
People are looking to buy it four or five times for agencies, but high growth agencies, they will pay like a six, a seven, an eight, and that's multiples of ebitda, by the way.
So that's just your profit margin.
Yep.
Okay.
Yeah, but let's stay in touch.
I think you would make a good proposition right now, but clearly you guys are still energized and you're young, so I should imagine you've probably got a couple of years in you in reality.
Yeah, yeah, that sounds about right.
But yeah, we'll certainly keep you, keep you posted on how this thing goes, but appreciate you taking the time for an intro chat.
Yeah, no worries.
No, it's good to get on your radar as well, but certainly if you run out of cash towards the end of the year, later, after your post wedding, then there may be an early sell.
Yeah, that's.
That's likely to happen.
We're going big.
We're going big in the doctor, so.
Oh, yeah, good, good.
Glad it wasn't just me.
My win is 12 years behind me now, but it's still very painful thinking about the amount of money.
Yeah.
So, all right.
Yeah, keep in touch with the edge.
I appreciate taking the time.
Have a good weekend.
Yeah, cheers.
Good luck.

Consider potential buyers for Greywolf Agency and keep in touch (28:01)
summary.overview: In the Introductory Business Meeting, Layton Lassiter from Greywolf Agency and Andrew Day from Capital A Group engaged in a fruitful discussion about Greywolf's unique positioning and future ambitions. Layton outlined the agency's specialization in PR for partnership and sponsorship marketing, notably its collaboration with Toyota, focusing on enhancing sponsorships through social media and earned media strategies. Greywolf has quickly established itself with notable clients and is approaching $1 million in revenue with a healthy profit margin. Plans for expansion include scaling the client roster and increasing headcount, with aspirations for industry marketing and thought leadership by 2025. Andrew provided insights on potential exit strategies and valuation estimates, emphasizing the importance of selling during a high growth phase. Action items included Layton's commitment to update Andrew on Greywolf's growth every six months and Andrew's intent to explore potential buyers for the agency.
summary.short_summary: During an introductory business meeting, Layton Lassiter from Greywolf Agency and Andrew Day from Capital A Group engaged in a productive dialogue regarding Greywolf's unique niche in public relations, particularly in partnership and sponsorship marketing. Layton highlighted the agency's successful collaborations, notably with Toyota, and its innovative approach to enhancing sponsorships through social media and earned media strategies. Greywolf has rapidly gained traction in the industry, nearing $1 million in revenue with a robust profit margin. Plans for future growth include expanding the client roster and increasing staff, with aspirations for becoming a leader in industry marketing and thought leadership by 2025. Andrew shared insights on exit strategies and valuation, underlining the significance of selling during periods of high growth. Action items included Layton's commitment to update Andrew on Greywolf's progress biannually and Andrew's plan to explore potential buyers.
